Documentation → Releases → 2.0.0

SATOM 2.0.0

A major release that adds Scout, the Fleet Calendar, Process, the Device Console, fleet-wide WAF views and a guided New Server Policy build, and removes two artifact controls.

👤 ForViewerOperatorAdministratorAdvanced user

Released: 2026-09-10 · All releases

In short#

SATOM 2.0.0 is the largest release so far. It adds tools for troubleshooting (Scout, the Device Console, Backend Reachability, Config Compare), for planning (the Fleet Calendar, scheduled HA failover, Process) and for seeing your whole FortiWeb estate (the Fleet WAF pages and a reworked WAF Artifacts area). It also introduces a guided way to build a server policy from a line, keeps the configuration change log forever, moves backups and snapshots off the node, and adds a container (Docker) installation.

It is numbered 2.0 rather than 1.21 because two controls were removed, not just hidden: the separate artifact management page and the Push this version to an appliance button. A bookmark or script that used either now gets a "not found" answer. See Before you upgrade.

What's new#

Troubleshooting#

Scout: find the layer that is actually broken#

Open Operations → Troubleshooting → Scout (FortiWeb) or Fleet → Scout (FortiADC), name one published object — a server policy or a virtual server — and Scout walks it from the bottom up. It stops at the first layer that fails and names it, with the evidence.

  • It checks, in order: appliance health; that the object exists and is enabled; that the published name resolves; that the front door answers (connection, TLS and time to first byte, shown separately); the certificate; the pool the device reports; the backends, seen from two vantage points that are never merged; the border firewall's record of the traffic (read from FortiAnalyzer logs); whether the appliance is deciding or just passing traffic through; and the WAF's recent blocks.
  • A check that could not run is counted as a blind spot. A walk with unchecked layers is reported as partial, never as healthy, and "we could not look" is never shown as a clean path.
  • Scout is read-only. It never changes anything on a device.
  • Scout is something you start for one object. Sentinel runs on its own schedule and picks its own objects; the two do not overlap.

Scout: pick the object from a list#

When you choose a FortiWeb or FortiADC, the name field now offers a drop-down of every server policy or virtual server.

  • The list combines what the appliance reports live with what SATOM collected in its last harvest, so a policy created minutes ago still appears. The list is grouped by where each entry came from, with the entries only one source knows about shown first.
  • When only one source could be read, entries are labelled as coming from one source only, rather than wrongly marked "not in the last harvest".
  • You can still type a name. This keeps devices that refuse to list their objects (for example an unlicensed FortiWeb VM) usable with Scout.
  • An empty list tells you why: the appliance answered and has no objects, or neither source could be read.
  • Long lists are capped at 400 entries and the page says how many were left out.

Scout: a clearer form with help on every field#

  • All twelve fields on the Scout form now have a ? explaining what to enter and how it changes the walk.
  • The fields are arranged in three visible sections — What to walk, Front door and Border correlation — instead of most of them being hidden in a collapsed panel.
  • The help for Port and Scheme now states that they are only used when you also type a Published host; otherwise they are taken from the device.
  • Five fields show that their default comes from Settings → Scout.

Device Console: run commands, test credentials, build a support bundle#

A new Device Console page in the Administrator menu of every ADOM lets you:

  • Run CLI commands against an appliance and read every answer. This is SATOM's first console that can make changes, and it is tightly guarded:
  • factory reset, log-disk formatting and disk erase are refused for everyone;
  • reboot, shutdown, configuration or firmware restore, HA changes, clear-text configuration exports and password changes are sent only after you confirm the effect and type the appliance name;
  • everything else needs configuration-write permission.
  • The whole script is checked before anything is sent, so a forbidden line at the end does not leave the first lines half-applied. By default the script stops at the first failed command, and lines that were not reached are reported as not run.
  • Test a username and password against a FortiOS device. The result tells you separately whether the device is reachable, whether the login worked and whether the account can actually read anything. Attempts are rate-limited per operator and audited; the password is never stored.
  • Package the session for Fortinet support (TAC). Secrets are removed from transcripts before they are stored or packaged. If a diagnostic capture fails, the bundle is still produced and notes the failure inside.

Backend Reachability: check many services at once#

A new Fleet page, Backend Reachability, takes a file or pasted list with one source;policy;destination per line and tells you, for each line, whether the real servers behind that policy answer — on the source appliance and then on the destination.

  • It changes nothing. It only pings from the appliances and opens test connections from SATOM, and each run is audited.
  • Every backend is reported as reachable, unreachable or unknown; each line gets a verdict of ok, down, mismatch, unknown or error. A probe that could not run is never shown as an outage or as healthy.
  • A problem on the destination side never hides the source result.
  • Source and destination pools are compared member by member, naming members missing from or extra on the destination. If the destination does not have the policy yet, the source's backends are pinged from the destination instead (useful before a migration), and the page says so.
  • Lines over the limit, targets beyond the 2000-target cap and backends skipped when time ran out are all named in the report.

Config Compare: is this service the same on both boxes?#

A new Fleet page, Config Compare, takes the same source;policy;destination list and compares everything behind each policy on both appliances: virtual server, server pool and members, certificates, content routing, allow-lists and the web protection profile.

  • Objects are matched by the role they play, not by name, so an object cloned under a different name is reported once as renamed rather than as "missing" plus "extra".
  • A web protection profile is compared as one package and summarised as which sub-profiles differ and by how much (removed, changed, added), instead of hundreds of individual rows.
  • Differences are found in both directions: a setting only the destination has counts as much as one only the source has.
  • Values that are bookkeeping on each box (such as internal row numbers) are ignored, and equivalent spellings such as enable and true are treated as the same.
  • A policy that is not on one of the boxes is reported as missing on that box.
  • Anything the comparison could not cover is named. The page is read-only, audited, and available in the Global and FortiWeb ADOMs. Results export as a tab-separated file, one line per difference.

Decommission a service from DNS & LB Lookup#

In DNS Lookup, the match that serves a name now has a Decommission button (FortiWeb and FortiADC ADOMs, configuration-write permission, always audited). One guarded pass removes the load-balancer object and what only it uses: the SNI entry, the certificate, the WAF profile, its exceptions and the DNS records pointing at the name.

  • You always see a preview first. When you confirm, SATOM checks the device again and refuses if anything changed since the preview, showing you the new plan.
  • If SATOM cannot confirm that nothing else uses an object, it keeps that object and tells you why.
  • Warnings that need your acknowledgement name the dependency — for example an SNI policy that still serves other domains, or a certificate that also covers other names.
  • DNS records are removed first, so a name is never left pointing at an address that may be reused.

Planning and automation#

Fleet → Calendar: everything scheduled, on one grid#

A new Fleet → Calendar page, first in the Fleet menu of every ADOM, shows month, week, 30-day agenda and full-year views of:

  • Planned changes — every change request, drawn across all the days of its window, with type, risk, appliances and owner;
  • Upcoming automations — recurring scheduled actions, projected forward;
  • What ran — recorded runs, so you can look back as well as forward.

You can plan a change straight from a day. It creates a normal change request, with all its usual checks. You can target an ADOM, a group (tag, department, zone or line) or named devices; a group is turned into a fixed list of appliances when the change is raised, and a group that matches nothing is refused. Two windows that overlap on the same appliance are flagged. Past days show only what actually ran. Anything the page leaves out (a capped series, a disabled automation, a clipped window) is stated. Days follow the timezone set in Settings → General.

Calendar: pick a day, expand it, or switch it off#

  • The whole day cell is clickable and the detail panel updates instantly. The page opens on today, and the address bar follows your selection so a link or refresh lands on the same day.
  • Any day can be expanded into a full-width window with the complete appliance list, every run time of a recurring job and the run summary. Warnings show in both the side panel and the expanded view.
  • You can switch the calendar off for yourself under My Profile → Calendar. It disappears from your Fleet menu only. Hiding it does not pause anything: approved changes and automations still run.

Calendar: choose what it shows#

A Show bar lets you tick Planned changes, Automations, System Automations and What already ran.

  • Hiding System Automations, for example, leaves your planned fleet work without a wall of nightly backups.
  • What already ran follows the groups above it: hiding a group hides its history too.
  • At least one of the first three always stays on, so the calendar can never be filtered empty.
  • Remember for me saves your choice to your profile. Filtering only changes what is drawn, never what you may open or do.
  • Day badges count everything, shown or hidden, so "hidden" and "nothing there" never look the same.

Automations and System Automations are now two pages#

Automation → Automations is a new page for fleet work people plan (a cutover, draining a backend, swapping a certificate). Automation → System Automations keeps SATOM's own housekeeping (backups, syncs, probe sweeps) at its existing address and permission.

  • Operators can now create their own automations: the new page needs configuration-write permission rather than user-management permission.
  • Every automation appears on exactly one of the two pages; anything with an unexpected scope lands on System Automations and is flagged for an administrator.
  • Calendar entries link to the page that owns them.
  • Both lists have a filter (name, action type, status, schedule) that you can save to your profile. Each page shows "Showing N of M", explains when a filter has emptied the list and offers a one-click Clear. A saved filter value that no longer exists is dropped and named. Unticking Remember for me forgets the saved filter.
  • If you hold the permission for the other page, Also show can display its rows here, read-only and linked to their own page.

HA failover: schedule it, or run it from the device page#

  • A new automation, HA failover: hand the primary role over, can be planned from Fleet → Calendar or from Change Requests. One direction hands the primary role to the peer; the other gives it back.
  • It always needs an approved change request and only runs inside its window.
  • It refuses firmware that cannot do it: on FortiWeb the failover command exists from 8.0.0, so a FortiWeb on 7.6 is refused by name with both version numbers and nothing is sent. FortiADC is supported from 7.6.0. A box with no recorded firmware version is refused too.
  • Handing over the primary role is refused on a box that is not primary right now. A node still reporting primary afterwards counts as a failure.
  • On FortiADC the forced state is treated as permanent until you give the role back, and every run says so.
  • A new HA Failover page on an HA cluster or member node (Appliances → your cluster → HA Failover) offers a readiness check that sends nothing, a live run, and planning. Standalone appliances are refused with advice on registering a cluster. A live run requires an approved change request window and the appliance name typed exactly. A change request approved for a firmware upgrade no longer authorises a failover of the same box, and the other way round.

Process: procedures SATOM walks for you#

Administrator → Process, in all five ADOM consoles. Draw a procedure once — a recovery plan, a post-upgrade check, an onboarding sequence — and SATOM walks it step by step and reports which step stopped it.

  • Thirteen step kinds, including HTTP, TCP (which tells a refused connection from a timeout), DNS, read-only console, appliance health, diagnostics collection, decision, manual approval gate, and the write-capable catalogue action, console script and integration hook.
  • Steps after a stop are recorded as skipped, never as passed; an unknown result makes the verdict partial; loops are allowed but bounded.
  • A run is a rehearsal unless you arm it. Unarmed, catalogue actions run as a dry run and console scripts and hooks are not sent.
  • A manual gate can wait hours for an answer. Each run keeps its own copy of the diagram, so editing a process never changes its past runs.
  • A process can be assigned to one or several ADOMs; with none it stays a draft visible only in Global.

Process: import and export as XML#

Administrator → Process → Import XML, and Export XML on any process page, let a procedure travel between installations or live in version control.

  • An imported process goes through exactly the same checks as one you draw, and is accepted whole or refused whole, with all problems listed together.
  • Drawing formats (draw.io, BPMN, Visio, SVG) are recognised and refused, because a drawing does not carry runnable steps.
  • An ADOM this installation does not have is an error. Replacing an existing process requires typing its key; run history is kept.
  • Export and re-import give back the same file. Reading and exporting need view permission; importing needs configuration-write permission.

FortiWeb WAF across the fleet#

Fleet → WAF: overview, inventory, profiles and coverage#

A new Fleet → WAF area (Global and FortiWeb consoles) shows every visible FortiWeb at once: an overview with key figures and six charts, every server policy, every web protection profile with its usage and gaps, and a protection-by-device coverage matrix. Each list exports to CSV.

  • The pages read SATOM's stored configuration snapshots and never contact a device, so they are fast. Freshness is shown as a column and a banner.
  • A device that was never harvested is named and left out of the figures; a snapshot older than 26 hours is marked stale but still shown.
  • Protection settings a profile does not have are shown as "not applicable" (grey), never as switched off.
  • The posture chart puts each policy in one bucket (disabled, no profile, monitor mode, blocking) and the totals beside it show overlaps the chart hides.
  • Findings — monitor mode, no profile, a profile reference that points nowhere, deprecated TLS, TLS without a certificate, disabled policies, unused profiles — come with the fix and a link to the rows concerned.

Fleet → WAF → Artifacts#

Every file-backed WAF object (XML Schema, DTD, WSDL, OpenAPI, gRPC IDL, JSON Schema, Lua) your estate uses or holds, in one table with six charts, breakdowns by type and scope, and a CSV of the filtered rows. Copies nobody uses are shown as orphans; empty copies are flagged; scopes never checked are shown as unknown, not zero.

Export the fleet view as one ZIP#

All five Fleet → WAF pages have an export panel. Tick the contents (overview and charts, server policies, protection profiles, coverage, artifacts, exceptions with their profiles) and the formats (CSV, Excel, PDF with the charts drawn in) and download one ZIP.

  • Exceptions become visible fleet-wide for the first time, each with the profile it belongs to, how many policies use that profile and its content.
  • Every file carries when it was made, by whom, how many scopes it covers, and which were stale or never harvested.
  • Charts come with their numbers as well as pictures.
  • The ZIP always covers the whole visible fleet; the per-table CSV link is the one that follows your filters.
  • Ticking nothing gives a message rather than an empty ZIP. Your selection is kept in the page link, so you can bookmark or share it.

WAF artifacts and exceptions#

A reorganised WAF Artifacts menu#

WAF Artifacts is now one collapsible sub-menu:

  • Object types — a statistics page for the device and ADOM you are on: how many web protection profiles carry files, how many policies use one, per-type figures, stored copies by origin, and a per-profile table. An ADOM never checked shows "never swept", not zeros. A banner names the device and ADOM shown (or "whole fleet") and explains that sibling ADOMs can legitimately show identical totals.
  • Inventory — what is held and what is needed, now with Device and ADOM columns. The Used on column is now a count. Upload, author and capture are three buttons with one dialog each. Every row has a view action, and the object page has a Back button that returns to your filtered list. Every action shows its purpose on hover.
  • Object page — view a file's content, edit it in place (each save is a new version) and compare any two versions.
  • Device audit — new: everything SATOM knows, grouped by device, exportable as JSON or CSV.

Artifacts know which profile and policy need them#

  • Every artifact reference now names the web protection profile it goes through, or says it belongs directly to the server policy (as Lua scripts do), or that it has not been worked out yet.
  • Each artifact gets one of four migration verdicts per device: ok (a copy for this device), borrowed (another appliance has a file with that name), at-risk (no copy, but still capturable from a live box) or blocked (no copy anywhere; the policy cannot be migrated until someone uploads the file).
  • Which policy needs which file is collected automatically, and a scheduled action refreshes it. A device that could not be reached never "proves" that its policies need nothing, and "never checked" is shown differently from "needs nothing".

Saving a shared file asks who it is for#

A file shared by several ADOMs is one file, so editing it "for production" used to change it for every ADOM. Now SATOM works out who a save will reach before writing and asks you to choose: all (a new version for everyone) or only (a separate copy for the device and ADOM you are on). Nothing is pre-selected. A separate copy stops receiving later edits of the shared one, and the page says so.

Custom signatures as exceptions#

  • Custom Signature is now a full exception type, with fields and values taken from a live FortiWeb rather than the admin guide's screen labels.
  • The operator choices now depend on the element type, so combinations the device rejects can no longer be authored.

Building server policies#

New Server Policy from a line#

A new wizard, linked from the policies page beside New Server Policy (Workspace → New Server Policy), builds a server policy from a line: the line's profile supplies the network, certificate class and web protection profile. IPAM reserves the address, DNS publishes the name, the CA issues the certificate and the device receives the objects, in that order.

  • Preview first. The plan writes nothing and lists every reason it cannot proceed, including a live check for name clashes on the device. A blocked plan is never applied.
  • A failure cleans up after itself. A DNS failure releases the address SATOM reserved; a device failure removes the DNS record and releases the address. An issued certificate is reported, not revoked, and objects already written to the device are listed rather than deleted. The report keeps "undone" and "left behind" apart.
  • No guessing. A segment the line does not receive is refused; with several segments you must choose; a blank hostname means "do not publish".
  • You can choose the IPAM backend and DNS backend to use. Both default to Auto, which behaves as before. A choice that is unknown, disabled, lacks the role or does not cover the request is refused, never quietly replaced by Auto. You are warned when a chosen backend would do nothing.
  • A Department control narrows the segment choice, segment options show the departments they serve, and the summary names the department.

Line Profiles#

A new Line Profiles page under Administrator (administrators only) declares, per line, the network segments it receives, its certificate class, its web protection profile template and an optional IPAM pool.

  • Lines without a profile still work by matching names, but the plan says it was inferred, not declared.
  • A profile that names a segment that no longer exists blocks the build rather than silently falling back.
  • A template's approval is checked when it is used, so a template rejected after the profile was saved can no longer be used.
  • A blank certificate class is reported as undecided.
  • Deleting or renaming a line accounts for its profile.

Several DNS and IPAM backends#

Settings → DNS Records is now a list of backends you can add, edit, enable or disable, test and delete. Each says whether it handles IPAM, DNS or both, and which zones and pools it serves.

  • The most specific match wins; priority breaks ties; an exact tie is refused and names the candidates.
  • No backend at all is supported and only warns. No match, or two equal matches, blocks the run, because it would publish somewhere nobody chose.
  • phpIPAM cannot be given the DNS role. A default zone or pool outside the backend's own scope is refused.
  • When there is a real choice, the +DNS Records window lets you pick the backend.
  • Rollback always works against the backend that did the work.

IPAM address allocation works#

Ticking allocate from IPAM now reserves an address on EfficientIP SOLIDserver, phpIPAM and NetBox. A Default IPAM pool field was added to all three provider forms. Rollback releases exactly the reservation SATOM made, even if the address has since been reused. These three integrations have been tested against simulations of each vendor's documented interface, not against real systems.

One network segment per network#

A network shared by two departments is now one segment listing both departments, instead of repeated rows. Duplicate segment names are refused when you save.

Cloning and the workspace#

Clone adds only what is missing#

The clone/migrate dialog has a new checkbox, on by default: an object the destination does not have is created in full, and an object it already has is left exactly as it is — no rows rewritten and no rows added. Rows held back are shown as untouched (amber) in the report. Changing the box invalidates the preview. A migration that held rows back leaves the source enabled. This mode cannot be combined with "new, compare and decide".

Workspace shows the device's own hostname#

The workspace now identifies an appliance by the hostname the device reports about itself, falling back to its address when none was ever reported (FortiAuthenticator does not report one). For a FortiWeb ADOM, the chassis hostname is shown and the tooltip explains it.

Stored Assets, Source of Truth and backups#

Stored Assets#

A new Stored Assets page in every ADOM shows, per device, the backups on the backup server with days since the last push, configuration snapshots split into local and off-box, firmware, identity and earlier names. It includes retired devices, folders on the server no device claims and configuration history with no known device.

  • "Never pushed" is its own state; an unreachable server shows as unknown, never as "no backups".
  • Deleting a backup needs the exact file name and typing DELETE; it is always audited and there is no bulk delete.
  • The page has four cards — device config backups, configuration SoT, firmware images and SATOM's own backup — under one filter bar. Device type, backup state, free text (including former names, serial, host and model) and hiding de-registered devices are kept in the page link. The backup-state filter only affects the first card, and that card says so.
  • Devices are grouped by product family, then by your own bookmark arrangement (line, zone, department), with the order shown and a link to change it in your profile. Unclassified groups sort last.
  • Every card and family starts folded, with counts on each heading, Expand all / Collapse all, and links that open a section directly. Warnings stay visible when folded, and a folded filter card still states the active filter.
  • SATOM's own bundles appear in Global only, marked as present on this node, on the backup server or both; a size mismatch between the two copies is flagged.

The configuration change log is kept, and snapshots leave the node#

  • The configuration Source of Truth no longer deletes change-log entries to save space, so you can always look back at an earlier value.
  • The bulky snapshot content now moves to the backup server instead. You set, per ADOM, how many recent versions (default 2) and days (default 1) stay on the node. Content is removed locally only after the backup server confirms it holds it, and older versions are fetched back automatically when you open or compare them.
  • A third setting, days of change log kept in the database (default 365, 0 = never trim), controls how long entries stay in the database. Before anything is removed, whole past months are archived to the backup server as one readable file per device and month, and nothing is removed unless the archive is confirmed at the right size.
  • Devices now record their serial number, and SATOM remembers device identities and former names even after a device is de-registered.

System bundles live off the node#

  • Backup Server → Local bundle retention (default 0): after a verified upload, the node keeps no local copy of its own system bundle. A local copy is deleted only when the server holds the same size. Download and restore fetch an off-box bundle automatically.
  • Backup Server → System bundle schedule: set the daily time of the system bundle, shown with the console's timezone. The change takes effect the same night, and the card shows the last and next run and warns if the schedule is disabled.

Settings: Source of Truth & Backup split in three#

The SoT & Backup settings tab is replaced by a Source of Truth & Backup group with Configuration SoT and Backup Server, plus Software Update Repository (formerly Git).

  • Configuration SoT has a new Refresh frequency (minutes between harvests, default 60, from 5 to 10080) and editable retention settings.
  • Each Backup Server path has a ? explaining what lands there and who writes it.
  • The repository form now sits inside the Repository card behind an Edit button, and opens by itself only on a node that has never had a repository registered.

Installation and the node#

A container (Docker) installation#

SATOM can now be installed as containers, alongside the full and package-only installations.

  • Four features that manage the host itself are deliberately switched off in this shape: in-place self-update, service control, certificate activation and systemd service health. Each tells you the alternative (restart the stack, deploy a new image version, install the certificate on the reverse proxy).
  • Production is a two-node cluster: a primary and a standby database replica. The standby refuses to rebuild a node that has been promoted, so data written after a failover is never lost.
  • The metrics store is not exposed outside the stack.
  • The installation guide and user guide now cover this shape, including the pages that behave differently on it.

HTTPS on every installation#

Every way of installing SATOM now sets up HTTPS itself, with an internal certificate authority and a node certificate. The certificate is self-signed, so your browser warns until you import your own; a certificate you imported is never overwritten by a later re-run, and a certificate that does not match its key is refused. Plain HTTP on port 80 now reliably redirects to HTTPS.

The satom console banner#

Running satom with no arguments now shows a SATOM wordmark, the version and node identity, and the licence statement. It shrinks to a one-line header in narrow terminals and can be turned off for runbooks.

What changes for you#

  • Artifact management moved. The separate artifact management page is gone; upload, author and capture are buttons on Inventory. The Push this version to an appliance button is gone: file content now reaches a device only when clone or migrate creates the object that uses it.
  • The migration-coverage table left the artifact Inventory. "Which policies can move today" is answered in the clone/migrate pre-flight checklist and in Device audit.
  • Artifact pages follow the device you selected. With a device and ADOM selected, the WAF Artifacts pages show only that pair; with none selected they send you to the map, as Backups does. The pickers offer only that pair, the Inventory appliance filter is replaced by a "held here / library" filter, and the Device audit device filter is gone. Old links that named a device switch your selected device to it.
  • Clone/migrate defaults to adding only what is missing. Untick the new checkbox to update existing objects as before.
  • Settings reorganised. SoT & Backup became Configuration SoT and Backup Server; Git became Software Update Repository (existing links still land). The firmware repository URL and branch settings were removed — firmware is managed under Infrastructure → Firmware.
  • Renamed buttons. "Apply the payload policy now" / "Push and evacuate now" are now Free space on this node now / Upload and free space now, and the card says plainly that history is not discarded.
  • Inactive ADOMs no longer get a SoT retention card; old overrides are listed with a Clear the override button.
  • Automations split into two pages, and operators can now create the user-level ones.
  • The Administration group is called Administrator in every ADOM's sidebar.
  • The DNS step of provisioning now has three outcomes: no provider still passes but says clearly that no name was published; a provider that cannot write records now fails.
  • The Calendar can be hidden per user and filtered; its entries open the page that owns them.

Fixed#

Scout - The report cut long lists (such as pool members) without saying so; it now states how many entries were left out. - The verdict label wrapped and looked cut off, and the submit button showed as plain text. - On FortiADC, Scout had no live view of virtual servers and could never report an empty device correctly. - The help could fail to load in an edge case instead of falling back.

Calendar and automations - The Calendar entry did nothing in the FortiADC console. - A saved calendar filter showed "part of your saved filter no longer exists" on every visit. - Hidden past runs were described as still firing; changing month could drop part of the filter; hidden items were left out of the counts. - A failover could never run on a cluster modelled per node; it was refused for "no recorded firmware version". - Giving the primary role back could not be scheduled, because a scheduled change lost its settings on rescheduling. - A change whose window ended before it began was accepted and then silently never ran; it is now refused.

Menus and navigation - In the FortiADC, FortiAnalyzer and FortiAuthenticator consoles, several menu entries (Device Console, AI Advisor, Stored Assets) led back to the ADOM home. - Choosing a FortiWeb cleared the FortiAuthenticator selection, and choosing the FortiAuthenticator made it the FortiWeb console's device. - An ADOM with a single appliance showed it on the dashboard but said "no device selected" on every other page. - The bookmarks rail said "Your session expired" in three ADOMs, broke after about an hour of use, and closed itself on every page change. - The Copy button on the error page could fail silently; it now shows why and selects the reference so you can copy it by hand.

Stored Assets - The page showed FortiWeb devices in every ADOM, including Global. - Each FortiWeb ADOM appeared as a separate device with a permanent "never pushed" badge.

Settings and backups - SoT retention settings never took effect; the built-in defaults were always used. - Saving a retention number could overwrite the backup server credentials and jump to another tab. - Saving the backup server form reset a custom system bundles path.

Server policies, DNS and IPAM - The New Server Policy wizard did nothing: the segment list stayed empty and Preview and Apply had no effect. The artifact editor was also unstyled. - A pool name with capital letters could never be matched. - Allocate from IPAM always failed, blaming a provider that was configured and working. - The DNS step always reported success, even when no record was published. - Two segments with the same name could make a plan describe one network while allocating from another. - The FortiADC Certificate column in DNS Lookup was always empty. - A real cascade delete showed an error page after the deletes had been made, instead of its report.

WAF artifacts and exceptions - Custom signatures were refused by the device at deploy time because five details were wrong (field names, operators, actions, severity and JSON Schema file names). Values the device would reject are now caught before deploy. - The detect button for artifacts did nothing. - An empty stored file was treated as ready to migrate and uploaded, leaving a rule that enforces nothing. Empty files are now warned about, kept apart from missing ones and refused without acknowledgement; uploads and captures that come back empty are refused. - Artifact pages labelled scopes with a management address instead of the device name. - With a device selected, artifact pages, their counters and their data feeds still showed or acted on the whole fleet, and a version could be opened or deleted by its number from another device. - A "this device only" save could create its copy on a different device. - The selected scope was lost when moving between artifact pages, and a scope that matched nothing silently showed the fleet. - An older exception type showed without a label and skipped validation; the catalogue had two names for the same condition.

Installation - Installations made with the other install scripts, and container installations, served plain HTTP, so no one could log in. A plain-HTTP setup now gets a message naming the real problem instead of "session expired". - The turnkey installer could fail at its last step when another website on the host was the default. - The installation guide pointed to a repository that no longer exists.

Before you upgrade#

  • Two artifact controls were removed. Bookmarks or scripts that opened the old artifact management page or used Push this version to an appliance will get "not found". There is intentionally no replacement for pushing a file on its own: content reaches a device when clone or migrate creates the object.
  • Backups leave the node by default. With Local bundle retention at 0, the node keeps no local system bundle after a verified upload, and snapshot content beyond 2 versions / 1 day moves to the backup server. Make sure your backup server is configured and reachable, and review these values per ADOM.
  • Change-log entries older than 365 days are archived to the backup server and then removed from the database. Set the value to 0 if you want to keep everything locally.
  • DNS Records settings are migrated automatically into one backend that covers everything, keeping your secret and default zone and pool.
  • Network segments: if you had one segment per department for the same network, merge them; a migration tool is provided and refuses to merge rows that disagree. Duplicate segment names are now refused.
  • Container installations: the old setting that published the application directly is retired and replaced by separate HTTPS and redirect address settings. The container helper stops and explains if it finds the old value, and also stops if the proxy's address does not match your trusted-proxy setting.
  • Clone/migrate now adds only what is missing by default.

Under the hood#

  • Sentinel and Scout now share one way of searching FortiAnalyzer logs.
  • Device Console transcripts are cleaned of secrets before they are stored, audited or packaged.
  • The artifact statistics page no longer scans every stored version on each load.
  • The release process's secret scan no longer blocks a publish over harmless placeholder text, while still catching real keys.
